sections.h2: How Kansas property tax is calculated
sections.html:
A Kansas tax bill comes in two steps. The county appraiser's estimate of fair market value, multiplied by an assessment rate, gives the assessed value. Take that assessed figure, apply the mill levy, and divide by 1,000 to arrive at the tax.

The residential assessment rate is 11.5%. Commercial property is assessed at 25% of full value. A mill equals $1 of tax for each $1,000 of assessed value. The levy stacks up the rates of every local taxing body, such as the school district, county and city. The county clerk can tell you the levy for your address.

The state's own teaching example uses a $200,000 home and a combined levy of 130 mills. Treat that as an illustration of the method, not a forecast for any particular house.

The Kansas year starts with valuation notices by March 1 and ends with the second half of the tax due on May 10 of the following year. These are the dates that matter most to a homeowner or a seller.

Kansas property tax calendar for real estate
DateEvent
March 1County mails valuation notices
30 days from mailingLast day to file an equalization appeal with the county appraiser
May 15Informal meeting with the county appraiser held by this date
May 20County appraiser gives final determination
June 1County appraiser certifies values to the county clerk
August 25Governing bodies certify budgets to the county clerk
November 1County clerk certifies the tax roll to the county treasurer
December 20Payment in full, or the first half, is due
May 10Second half due

Personal property follows a separate schedule, with its own valuation notice date of May 1.

Each taxing unit sets its own levy from its budget. The revenue neutral rate is the mill levy that, applied to the current year's assessed valuation, would produce the same property tax revenue as the prior year.

Public steps are built into the calendar around it. The county clerk reports the rate for each taxing jurisdiction by June 15. A governing body that wants to go above it tells the county clerk by July 20 and holds a public hearing between August 20 and September 20. That hearing window is the best time for a homeowner to speak up about a rising bill, because budgets are certified by August 25.

The levy is one reason two houses with the same appraised value can carry different bills. A house in one school district or city can sit under a higher combined levy than a house a few blocks away in another. Buyers notice this, so know your own levy before you set a price.

You have two routes, and for a given tax year you must choose one: an equalization appeal after the spring notice, or payment under protest when you pay.

  • Equalization appeal: reach out to the county appraiser inside 30 days of the notice's mailing date, then go to the informal meeting, which must happen by May 15.
  • Third-party appraisal option: after the informal result, the owner may file a fee simple appraisal done by a Kansas certified appraiser inside 60 days after the notice went out. The county then has 90 days to respond.
  • Payment under protest: hand the protest form to the county treasurer at the time you pay. December 20 is the cutoff, even if you are paying only the first half.

An informal meeting that fails to settle things sends you on to the Board of Tax Appeals. A single-family residence must go to the BOTA Small Claims Division first, and so must a non-agricultural property valued under $3 million. One hearing officer hears small claims appeals, and the appeal form usually comes with the notice of informal meeting results. Each filing deadline is 30 days after the earlier decision was mailed.

sections.h2: What happens when the tax goes unpaid
sections.html:
Unpaid Kansas real estate tax draws interest and, after enough time, can lead to a county foreclosure sale. Under K.S.A. 79-2004 you can pay everything by December 20 or split the bill, with the second half landing on May 10. A deadline on a weekend rolls to the next business day. A bill of $10 or less must be paid whole on December 20.

If the first half is missed, interest starts at the K.S.A. 79-2968 rate, with five percentage points added each year. Taxes still unpaid after May 10 draw the same rate until paid or until the property is sold for taxes by foreclosure.

Foreclosure comes later. Under K.S.A. 79-2801, when property the county bought at sale remains unredeemed on September 1 of the second year afterward, the county attorney is directed to file an action in district court. The law makes that action discretionary where the aggregate assessed valuation is under $300,000 or the delinquent taxes and special assessments are under $10,000. If the county does not act on property inside a city and the taxes have stayed delinquent for three years after the property became eligible, the city may start the foreclosure itself.

If a delinquency notice has already arrived, read it closely and call the county treasurer right away about redemption.

sections.h2: Selling with taxes owed, and tax steps at closing
sections.html:
At closing, the title company usually pays this year's tax and any back taxes out of your proceeds. A tax lien follows the house to a new owner, so it has to be cleared first. Request a payoff figure from the title company well before the closing date.

  • The recorded deed must show the buyer's name and mailing address. The register of deeds passes that address to the county clerk so tax statements reach the right person (K.S.A. 58-2221).
  • A deed generally needs a sales validation questionnaire. K.S.A. 79-1437f keeps sale prices off the public record.
  • Questions about a specific property's value belong with the county appraiser, and the county treasurer answers payment questions.

If a house has delinquent taxes, a repair backlog or a probate hold, our team can look at it as-is. A title company will ask about the same tax points, so have your latest tax statement in hand when you call.

Before listing, pull your latest valuation notice and tax statement, confirm whether the first half is paid, and check whether an appeal or protest is open for this year.

faqs.q: When are Kansas property taxes due?
faqs.a: Real estate tax is due in full by December 20, or in two halves with the first by December 20 and the second by May 10 of the next year (K.S.A. 79-2004). A due date on a weekend moves to the next business day.

faqs.q: How long do I have to appeal my Kansas valuation?
faqs.a: Thirty days from the date the county mailed the notice of value. The notice goes out by March 1, so the window usually closes in spring. The informal meeting with the county appraiser must be held by May 15.

faqs.q: Can I appeal and also pay under protest?
faqs.a: No. A taxpayer picks one path for the same tax year: appeal at the valuation notice or pay under protest, not both.

faqs.q: What is the residential assessment rate in Kansas?
faqs.a: Residential property is assessed at 11.5% of appraised value. The assessed value is then multiplied by the combined mill levy and divided by 1,000 to produce the tax.

faqs.q: Who do I contact about my Kansas property tax bill?
faqs.a: The county appraiser handles value questions, the county clerk holds the mill levy, and the county treasurer takes payments and the payment under protest form.
